newsitem.title: USA: Steady U.S. rates shows Fed betting on slowdown.
newsitem.headline: Steady U.S. rates shows Fed betting on slowdown.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's decision on Wednesday to leave short-term interest rates unchanged indicated the central bank expects the economy to slow down from its torrid fourth-quarter pace, analysts said.
"They are gambling the economy will slow down and inflation will remain dormant," said Astrid Adolfson, senior economist at MCM MoneyWatch.
Adolfson noted that inflation, the Fed's chief concern, did not pick up in 1996, a year marked by above-trend growth and full employment.

The Gross Domestic Product rose by 4.7 percent in October-December and was up 3.4 percent, fourth-quarter over fourth-quarter, for all of 1996. Fed officials have repeatedly stated the non-inflationary pace of the economy is between 2.0 percent and 2.5 percent.
The unemployment rate has remained under 5.50 percent since May -- lower than the non-inflationary jobless rate most economists put at 5.75 percent.
"But they probably still have a tightening bias," said Adolfson, referring to the Fed's directive introduced in July to allow an inter-meeting move.
"The likelihood of a spring tightening remains. They'll move as soon as they see signs of inflation or if there are inflation fears in the market," Adolfson added.
Following the Fed's announcement, the 30-year Treasury bond extended its losses to 12/32, reflecting market concern about inflationary risks.
But Adolfson pointed out one key consideration at the Fed that may have accounted for the absence of a rate hike was the level of the real, inflation-adjusted, federal funds rate.
"The real funds rate is not far from where it should be," the MCM MoneyWatch senior economist said.
The Fed last eased credit just over a year ago when it lowered the discount and funds rates by 25 basis points -- a move it described as an anti-recession "insurance."
The 5.25-percent funds rate, adjusted for inflation, remains slightly on the firm side by historic standards.

Chief economist David Resler at Nomura Securities International said the Fed will be watching for the early 1997 economic data to consider its policy -- and be ready to move, including inter-meeting, at the first sign of inflation.
"One must be cautious in concluding that no action now precludes any move later in the quarter," Resler said.

"Such decision will be dictated by the events of the coming weeks, mainly the January employment report and retail sales," added Resler, who saw the possibility of an inter-meeting move in late February, following Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress.
The January jobs data are due out Friday, February 7 at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Jim Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities, also focused on the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, where he expected "Greenspan to forecast growth will slow."

"They want to be preemptive, meaning they have to respond before the stage is set for inflation. Yet, they do care about what the public thinks, and until they see some signs of an inflation problem, they seem inclined to wait."
